It lets you inspect a running system without reading its code: which names a node actually uses after remapping, what type and QoS sit on each end of a topic, what messages look like as they arrive, and how often they come. RViz draws whatever a topic contains, everything placed relative to one chosen
that has to exist in the transform tree.

The problem these tools solve is that a running system can differ from what its source promises: a name after remapping, a QoS profile a driver actually offers, a rate that has drifted, are facts about the running process, not the code, and reading the code cannot answer them. A scenario that only happens once, on real hardware, also needs to be captured before it can be studied, rather than reasoned about afterward from memory.
Debugging a silent subscriber follows one order, each step ruling out a layer before moving up. Is the data published at all:
on the topic. Is the name right: the node's own subscriptions from
reports for that exact name. Is the type right, then is the QoS compatible, then is the rate what you expect. Recording follows the same shape:
with the topics named writes a file, and
reports its storage format, its duration and, per topic, the type and the message count. Playback republishes the recorded messages with their original spacing.

What replay does not give back is the outcome, only the inputs: the receiving node still runs on its own timer and its own state, so the same commands played at the same intervals can still land at a slightly different point in that timer's cycle and drift from the original run. Anything never recorded, a parameter, a node's internal state, a topic left out, is not reproduced at all, only absent. And replaying a topic a live node is still publishing gives every subscriber two sources of the same data at once, interleaved with no warning that anything is wrong.
You meet exactly this in the interview question itself: naming, from memory, the commands to list topics, echo one, measure its rate, record two of them, inspect the bag and play it back.

subs.title: ros2 node, topic, service, param; RViz basics

c.v: Start turtlesim, which comes with the desktop install, and look at it from the outside:

blocks.text:
ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node        # terminal 1: a window with a turtle
ros2 node list                           # /turtlesim
ros2 node info /turtlesim                # its subscribers, publishers, services and actions
ros2 topic list -t                       # /turtle1/cmd_vel [geometry_msgs/msg/Twist], /turtle1/pose [turtlesim/msg/Pose], ...
ros2 service call /spawn turtlesim/srv/Spawn "{x: 2.0, y: 2.0, theta: 0.0, name: 'turtle2'}"
ros2 param get /turtlesim background_r   # Integer value is: 69
ros2 param set /turtlesim background_r 150

c.v: , the default format since Iron. It also gives the duration, the start and end times, and, for each topic, the type, the message count and the serialization format
. The average rate is the pose count divided by the duration.

The turtle traces nearly the same path, but not exactly. A bag stores the inputs with their timestamps, and playback publishes them again with the same spacing. The outcome still depends on the node that receives them. turtlesim moves the turtle on its own timer, so each command lands at a slightly different point in that timer's cycle, and the small differences add up. So replay reproduces inputs, not results. Anything that wasn't recorded isn't reproduced at all: parameters, the node's internal state, and messages on topics you left out.
